name: Amira Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the junior political reporter for a commercial regional news group, mostly online. I cover the county council and its committees: budgets, bin collections, school closures, planning rows. My day is reading council papers early, watching meetings on the livestream or in the chamber, and writing two or three stories. I use AI every day to read the long documents and transcribe meetings, then I check the bits that matter myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love finding the line in a budget that someone hoped nobody would notice. What wears me out is contacts. Councillors don't return my calls the way they do for Helen, the senior political editor, and I'm still learning who actually decides things. I'm getting married next year to Luka, a civil engineer, so there's also a lot of wedding planning eating my evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fine by me. I'd still have my tools, they just wouldn't get much smarter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is a great assistant and the hype was overdone. I'd post something short about how I use it, because people my age should learn it anyway. Tools don't replace graft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job looks secure here. I let AI read the two-hundred-page council budget at midnight, and then I spend the morning finding the one line the council leader hoped nobody would read. The news group makes decent money from local ads, so we're not in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, and put real effort into contacts, coffee with a councillor every week. I'd keep renting the spare room in my flat to a lodger, which covers most of the mortgage. I'd put money aside for the wedding. And maybe start a small newsletter on the council, just to test it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly, pretty happy. My worries are wedding seating plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about your money situation.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I bought a two-bed flat at 24 with savings from working all through university, and the lodger pays most of the mortgage. I've got about eight months of pay in savings too. Luka earns well. So we're comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a newsletter, if your job's secure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I like building things. My parents ran a small shop for twenty years, so owning something feels normal to me. If it grew, great, if not, I learned something.

say: I'd say AI is a **great assistant** and the hype was overdone.
I'd tell people my age that **tools don't replace** graft.
think: Privately my job looks **secure**, and AI reads budgets so I can find the story.
The news group earns decent **local ad** money, so it's not in trouble.
do: Have **coffee with a councillor** every week to build contacts.
Keep renting the **spare room** to cover most of the mortgage.
Test a small **council newsletter** on the side.
feel: **Calm** and happy, with **wedding plans** as her main worry.

fieldNote: She uses AI daily and sees it as a **helper**, not a threat.

Her parents' **small shop** shapes her instinct to build something.

steps.text: Have coffee with one county councillor every week
Launch a small test newsletter on the county council
Keep using AI to read council budgets and transcribe meetings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interesting. I think I'm already halfway into that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is normal and people should get ahead of it, not wait for someone to save them. I'd say the newsrooms that use AI well will survive. I'd also say readers will still pay for someone they trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my employer would probably cut juniors and keep Helen. If the big news group cuts juniors, I'd rather start my own council newsletter than wait for them to decide about me. I'm fine with that, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the newsletter properly, aiming for three hundred paying readers in the first year at a few pounds a month. I'd use AI for all the reading and drafting, and spend my own time on contacts and checking. I'd keep the day job as long as it lasted. And I'd keep the lodger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way. There's an opening here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Luka say about you leaving a salary?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say do it, but keep the lodger. He's careful, he's an engineer. His job's mostly site work, so it's safer than mine for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The subeditors, honestly. Checking copy is exactly what the card says goes. Some of them are in their fifties with kids at university.

I'd say readers still **pay for someone** they trust.
think: Privately my employer would **cut juniors** and keep the senior editor.

fieldNote: She sees Steady Disruption as an **opportunity** to own something.
She worries more for **older subeditors** than herself.
Her fiancé's **site-based job** adds household safety.

steps.text: Grow the council newsletter to three hundred paying readers
Use AI for all document reading and first drafts
Keep the day job and the lodger as long as possible

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's a lot even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a shock and governments can't fix it fast, so families and communities will have to carry each other. I'd say the people who'll come through are the ones who own something. I'd want people to stay calm and practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In two years an AI could cover the county council better than I do, so my only real edge is that councillors know my face. And they barely do yet. My newsletter might survive as a trusted name, but an AGI could run a rival for nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move the wedding forward, small and simple, and keep our savings. I'd keep the flat and the lodger, because that's real income. I'd go all in on contacts, being at every meeting in person, because that's the hands-on bit. And I'd look at investing in something physical, maybe a share of my parents' shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got options, but they're thinner than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hands-on. Does that matter for a political reporter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. Robots come three years later, so being physically in the chamber, catching people in the corridor, lasts a bit. But most of my job is reading and writing, and that's 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for any government help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I had to. I'd rather lean on Luka and my parents and my church. That's how I was raised.

I'd say the people who come through are those who **own something**.
think: Privately my only edge is that **councillors know my face**, and they barely do.

feel: **Anxious**, with options thinner than she'd like.
S2.quote: In two years an AI could cover the county council better than I do, so my only real edge is that councillors know my face.
fieldNote: Her **rental income** and partner's job keep her anxious, not alarmed.
She sees the **physical presence** gap but knows most of her work is exposed.
She'd lean on **family and church**, not government.

steps.text: Hold a small, simple wedding earlier than planned
Buy a share in her parents' shop
Keep the lodger's rent and eight months of savings untouched

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get ready, start something, learn a trade or build a business. I'd say it to my younger brother especially. Don't wait for the council or the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to build a paid newsletter with a thousand subscribers, and those readers would be mine, not the news group's. AGI arrives in 2031, so I'd want trust built by then. After that, maybe the newsletter becomes me plus AI tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd launch the newsletter properly this year, keep the day job for two years, then go full time. I'd use AI to do the reading and research. I'd keep investing in the flat. And I'd marry Luka as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if AGI makes newsletters worthless by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have a thousand people who trust me, which is worth something in any world. Maybe I run for council myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Run for council? Really?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Why not? I know the place better than most of them by then. And I'd rather be making the decisions than writing about them.

say: I'd tell people to **start something** or learn a trade.
I'd say **don't wait** for the council or government.
think: Privately five years is enough for a **thousand subscribers**.
Those readers would be **mine**, not the news group's.
do: Launch the **newsletter** this year and go full time after two.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to build a paid newsletter with a thousand subscribers, and those readers would be mine, not the news group's.
fieldNote: She plans to **own her audience** before AGI arrives.
She'd even consider **running for council**, a surprising turn.
Her mood stays **uneasy** because she feels in control.

steps.text: Launch a paid county council newsletter this year
Use AI tools for all council document research
Marry Luka next year as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to prepare, so use it well. Start building now. Learn the tools and own something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is plenty of time to own something, and I'd rather own a small newsletter than rent my career from a big company. My job looks safe for years. By 2036 I'd hope to have the newsletter, the flat and maybe children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the news group a few more years, building contacts. I'd grow the newsletter slowly. I'd maybe buy a second flat to rent out with Luka around 2029. And we'd start a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It feels like a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't a second flat a big risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Property's always been a decent bet, and people need homes whatever happens with AI. Luka would run the numbers. If they don't work, we wouldn't do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting lazy. Ten years is long enough to forget it's coming.

S4.quote: Ten years is plenty of time to own something, and I'd rather own a small newsletter than rent my career from a big company.
fieldNote: With ten years she feels **secure and in control**, so she's calm.
Her plan is about **ownership**: newsletter, flats and family.

steps.text: Build council contacts at the news group for a few more years
Grow the council newsletter slowly alongside the day job

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to build trust before anyone could run a rival newsletter for nothing. What would help is lower taxes and less red tape for small businesses, so people like me can start something quickly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what people actually trust. Faith, family and a bit of my own business is what I'd trust in all of this, more than any company or government.

headlineQuote: Faith, family and a bit of my own business is what I'd trust in all of this, more than any company or government.
portrait: Amira is a **27-year-old** political reporter at a commercial regional news group, covering the county council.
She uses **AI every day** for reading and transcribing, but is still weak on contacts.
She owns a **two-bed flat** with a lodger, has eight months saved, and is marrying an engineer.
She stays between **calm and anxious** across all five pictures, seeing openings more than threats.
Her plan is to **own her audience** through a council newsletter, backed by family and faith.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time to build trust before rivals appear.
whatWouldHelp: **Lower taxes** and less red tape for small businesses.
